lessons.title: Types of Joints: Butt, Lap, T, Corner, Edge
lessons.body:
When you join two pieces of metal, the way you arrange them before welding is called the joint type. The five basic joints are butt, lap, T, corner, and edge. Each has a specific use and requires different preparation. For a butt joint, you place two plates edge to edge in the same plane. This is the most common joint for pipes and plates. You need to bevel the edges for thick metal (over 6 mm) to ensure full penetration. A root gap of 1.5â3 mm is typical. In Africa, many workshops use oxy-fuel cutting to bevel edges, then grind them clean.

A lap joint overlaps one plate on another. It's strong and easy to align, often used for sheets and structural work. You weld along the edge of the top plate. For a T-joint, one plate stands perpendicular to another, forming a 'T'. This is common in frames and beams. You can weld from one or both sides. A corner joint joins two plates at an angle, like a box corner. You can weld inside, outside, or both. An edge joint places two plates side by side and welds along the edges; it's used for thin sheets and not for high stress.

In practice, you must clean all joints to bare metal before welding. Remove rust, paint, and oil with a grinder or wire brush. For a butt joint on 10 mm plate, use a 60Â° included angle bevel, a 2 mm root gap, and a 3 mm root face. For a T-joint on 8 mm plate, a 45Â° bevel on the vertical plate works well. Always tack weld first to hold alignment. In rural Africa, where power can be unreliable, a generator welder (e.g., 5 kW) is common. Use 3.2 mm electrodes at 90â120 amps for these joints. Remember: joint design controls strength. A poorly fitted joint will fail, no matter how good your welding.

lessons.title: Welding Positions: Flat, Horizontal, Vertical, Overhead
lessons.body:
The position you weld in changes everything: gravity pulls molten metal down, so you must adjust your technique. The four standard positions are flat (1G), horizontal (2G), vertical (3G), and overhead (4G). Flat is easiest: you weld on top of a plate, and gravity helps the metal flow into the joint. Use higher current and a drag angle (electrode tilted 5â15Â° away from direction of travel). For 3.2 mm electrode, set 110â140 amps. This is where you learn.

Horizontal position: you weld on a vertical surface but the weld axis is horizontal. The molten metal tends to sag. Use a slight backhand angle (electrode tilted 0â10Â° toward the weld) and lower current, about 90â110 amps for 3.2 mm. Keep a short arc and move steadily. Vertical: you weld up or down a vertical plate. Vertical-up gives better penetration but is slower; vertical-down is faster but prone to lack of fusion. For vertical-up, use 80â100 amps, a slight weave, and pause at the sides. Overhead: you weld from below, fighting gravity. Use the lowest current, 70â90 amps for 3.2 mm, and a very short arc. Keep the puddle small and move quickly.

In Africa, many welders work on pipelines, water tanks, and gates in all positions. Practice each position on scrap plates. A good exercise: take two 10 mm plates, tack them in a T, and run beads in all four positions. Check your penetration by cutting and etching with acid (or just break it). Remember: position affects heat input. Overhead and vertical need less heat to avoid dripping. Always wear a leather apron and sleevesâsparks fly downward in overhead. If you're welding a water tank in a village, you might have to do vertical and overhead welds on the inside. That's where skill matters.

lessons.title: Visual Inspection of Welds
lessons.body:
Visual inspection is the first and most important check of any weld. Before you weld, inspect the joint: are the edges clean, the gap correct, and the parts aligned? After welding, look for defects with your naked eye and a magnifying glass (10x). You need good lightâuse a torch or daylight. Check for uniform bead size, smooth ripples, and proper tie-in at the toes. A good weld has a slight crown (1â2 mm high) and no undercut. Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal along the weld edge; it weakens the joint. Measure it with a welding gauge if you have one.

Look for cracks, porosity (small holes), slag inclusions (dark spots), and incomplete fusion. Cracks can be hairline; clean the surface with a wire brush and look again. Porosity appears as tiny pits or holes on the surface. Slag inclusions look like dark lines or spots. Incomplete fusion shows as a gap between weld and base metal. Also check for spatterâsmall metal balls stuck to the surface. Spatter is not a defect but indicates wrong current or arc length. For critical welds, use a fillet weld gauge to measure leg length. A 6 mm fillet weld should have 6 mm legs.

In Africa, many workshops lack expensive testing equipment, so visual inspection is your main tool. Train your eye: weld a test piece, then break it in a vice. Look at the fracture surfaceâif you see shiny metal, it's fused; if you see dark, rough areas, it's not. Keep a log of your inspections. For structural work, codes like AWS D1.1 require 100% visual inspection. You can make a simple checklist: no cracks, no undercut over 0.8 mm, porosity less than 3 mm, and proper size. Always inspect before, during, and after welding. If you see a defect, grind it out and reweld. Never paint over a bad weld.

lessons.title: Common Weld Defects and Causes
lessons.body:
Every welder makes defects; the key is to know why and how to fix them. The most common defects are porosity, slag inclusion, lack of fusion, undercut, overlap, and cracks. Porosity is gas trapped in the weld, appearing as small holes. Causes: damp electrodes, dirty base metal, too long an arc, or wrong polarity. Fix: use dry electrodes (store in a heated quiver at 100â150Â°C), clean metal, and shorten arc. Slag inclusion is slag trapped in the weld, often from poor cleaning between passes. Use a chipping hammer and wire brush after each pass.

Lack of fusion: the weld metal doesn't fuse to the base metal or previous pass. Causes: low current, fast travel, wrong electrode angle, or too large a root gap. Increase current by 10â20 amps, slow down, and direct the arc at the joint. Undercut: a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe. Causes: too high current, long arc, or wrong angle. Reduce current, shorten arc, and use a slight backhand angle. Overlap: weld metal rolls over the base metal without fusing. Causes: low current, fast travel, or wrong angle. Increase current and slow down. Cracks: can be hot (during solidification) or cold (after cooling). Causes: high sulfur in steel, rapid cooling, or high restraint. Preheat thick steel to 100â150Â°C and use low-hydrogen electrodes like E7018.

In Africa, humidity is a common cause of porosityâelectrodes absorb moisture. Always keep electrodes in a sealed container with silica gel. For field work, use a portable oven (12V or gas). Also, rusty plates are common; grind to shiny metal. If you see a defect, grind it out completely (to sound metal) and reweld. Never weld over a defect. For critical jobs like bridges or pressure vessels, use a qualified welding procedure. Remember: 80% of defects come from poor preparation and wrong current. Check your machine settings daily with a test bead.

lessons.title: Introduction to Non-Destructive Testing
lessons.body:
Non-destructive testing (NDT) finds defects without damaging the weld. The main methods are visual (VT), dye penetrant (PT), magnetic particle (MT), ultrasonic (UT), and radiographic (RT). In Africa, VT is everywhere; PT and MT are affordable for workshops; UT and RT are expensive and usually only for critical projects like pipelines or pressure vessels. Dye penetrant works on clean, smooth surfaces. You spray a red penetrant, wait 10 minutes, wipe it off, then spray a white developer. Red lines show cracks or porosity. It costs about $20 for a kit and works on stainless and aluminum. Magnetic particle testing uses a magnetic field and iron powder. It only works on ferromagnetic metals (steel). You magnetize the part, spray iron powder, and defects show as powder clusters. A yoke kit costs $200â500.

Ultrasonic testing sends high-frequency sound waves into the weld. A transducer picks up echoes from defects. It requires training and a calibrated machine ($2000+). Radiographic testing uses X-rays or gamma rays to produce a film image. It's the most reliable but needs a license and radiation safety. In many African countries, RT is done by specialized companies. For a small workshop, start with VT and PT. PT can find surface cracks that VT misses. MT is better for subsurface defects near the surface. Always clean the weld before PT or MTâoil and paint will block penetration.

If you can't afford NDT, use destructive testing on test pieces: bend tests, nick-break tests, or macro-etch. For a bend test, cut a strip across the weld, bend it in a vice; if it cracks, the weld is bad. Macro-etch: polish a cross-section, apply acid (e.g., 10% nitric acid in alcohol), and look at the fusion line. In Africa, many welders use the 'hammer and chisel' test: chisel along the weld toe; if it lifts, lack of fusion. But for code work, you need certified NDT. Consider partnering with a local NDT company for critical jobs. Always document results.

lessons.title: Weld Quality Standards and Codes
lessons.body:
Welding codes are rules that ensure safety and quality. The most common international codes are AWS D1.1 (structural steel), ASME Section IX (pressure vessels), and ISO 9606 (welder qualification). In Africa, many countries adopt these or have their own, like SANS 10162 in South Africa. A code tells you: joint design, electrode type, preheat, current range, and acceptance criteria. For example, AWS D1.1 says for a 10 mm fillet weld, you must use a minimum leg size of 5 mm, and undercut cannot exceed 0.8 mm. It also requires welders to be qualified by testing.

To qualify a welder, you weld a test coupon according to a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS). The WPS lists all variables: process (SMAW), electrode (E7018), current (110â140 A), position (3G), and joint design. Then the coupon is tested by visual, bend, and sometimes RT. If it passes, you get a certificate for that position and thickness. In Africa, many welders learn on the job without certification. But for jobs like building a bridge or a fuel tank, clients demand certified welders. You can get certified through organizations like the African Welding Federation or local training centers. It costs $100â500.

In your workshop, create a simple quality plan: use a checklist for each job. Check base metal (clean, correct grade), electrode (dry, correct type), machine settings, and welding technique. After welding, inspect visually. For critical welds, hire an NDT inspector. Keep records: date, welder name, WPS number, and inspection results. If a defect is found, repair it and re-inspect. Remember: codes are not just paperworkâthey prevent failures that kill people. A poorly welded trailer hitch can cause a fatal accident. Follow the code, even if it slows you down. In Africa, where infrastructure is growing, quality welding builds trust and gets you better-paying jobs.

quiz.q: Which joint type places two plates edge to edge in the same plane?
quiz.explanation: A butt joint aligns two plates edge to edge in the same plane.

quiz.q: What is the typical root gap for a butt joint on 10 mm steel plate?
quiz.explanation: A root gap of 1.5â3 mm allows proper penetration in a butt joint.

quiz.q: Which joint is most common for pipes and plates?
quiz.explanation: Butt joints are widely used for pipes and plates due to their strength and simplicity.

quiz.q: What is the included angle for a single-V butt joint on 10 mm plate?
quiz.explanation: A 60Â° included angle is standard for a single-V butt joint on 10 mm plate.

quiz.q: Which joint is best for thin sheets and not for high stress?
quiz.explanation: Edge joints are used for thin sheets and are not designed for high-stress applications.

quiz.q: In which welding position does gravity help the molten metal flow into the joint?
quiz.explanation: In the flat position, gravity assists the molten metal to flow into the joint.

quiz.q: What is the typical current range for a 3.2 mm electrode in the flat position?
quiz.explanation: Flat position allows higher current, typically 110â140 A for a 3.2 mm electrode.

quiz.q: Which position requires the lowest current to prevent dripping?
quiz.explanation: Overhead welding fights gravity, so the lowest current is used to keep the puddle small.

quiz.q: What is the recommended current for vertical-up welding with a 3.2 mm electrode?
quiz.explanation: Vertical-up requires lower current, typically 80â100 A, to control the puddle.

quiz.q: Which welding position is done on a vertical surface with the weld axis horizontal?
quiz.explanation: Horizontal position is on a vertical surface with the weld axis horizontal.

quiz.q: What is the first and most important check of any weld?
quiz.explanation: Visual inspection is the first and most fundamental method for checking weld quality.

quiz.q: What does undercut look like on a weld?
options: A) A groove melted into the base metal along the weld edge
B) Small holes on the surface
C) Dark spots inside the weld
D) A crack along the weld center
quiz.explanation: Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowed undercut in AWS D1.1 for most applications?
quiz.explanation: AWS D1.1 typically limits undercut to 0.8 mm for most structural applications.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to measure the leg length of a fillet weld?
quiz.explanation: A fillet weld gauge is specifically designed to measure fillet weld leg lengths.

quiz.q: What does a shiny, smooth fracture surface on a broken weld indicate?
quiz.explanation: A shiny, smooth fracture surface indicates good fusion between weld and base metal.

quiz.q: Which defect appears as small holes on the weld surface?
quiz.explanation: Porosity appears as small holes or pits on the weld surface.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of porosity in welding?
quiz.explanation: Damp electrodes release gas during welding, causing porosity.

quiz.q: How can you prevent slag inclusion?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning between passes with a chipping hammer and wire brush prevents slag inclusion.

quiz.q: What causes lack of fusion?
quiz.explanation: Too low current prevents proper melting and fusion with the base metal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended preheat for thick steel to avoid cracks?
quiz.explanation: Preheating thick steel to 100â150Â°C helps prevent cold cracks.

quiz.q: Which NDT method uses a red penetrant and white developer?
quiz.explanation: Dye penetrant testing uses a red penetrant and white developer to reveal surface defects.

quiz.q: Which NDT method only works on ferromagnetic metals?
quiz.explanation: Magnetic particle testing requires the material to be ferromagnetic, like steel.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a dye penetrant testing kit?
quiz.explanation: A basic dye penetrant kit costs around $20, making it affordable for small workshops.

quiz.q: Which NDT method requires a license and radiation safety?
quiz.explanation: Radiographic testing uses X-rays or gamma rays and requires a license and safety measures.

quiz.q: What is a simple destructive test for weld quality?
quiz.explanation: A bend test is a simple destructive test that reveals lack of fusion or cracks.

quiz.q: Which code covers structural steel welding?
quiz.explanation: AWS D1.1 is the code for structural steel welding.

quiz.q: What does a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) list?
options: B) Variables like current and electrode
quiz.explanation: A WPS lists all essential variables such as process, electrode, current, and position.

quiz.q: What is the minimum leg size for a 10 mm fillet weld according to AWS D1.1?
quiz.explanation: AWS D1.1 requires a minimum leg size of 5 mm for a 10 mm fillet weld.

quiz.q: How can a welder get certified in Africa?
options: A) Through the African Welding Federation
B) By buying a certificate online
quiz.explanation: The African Welding Federation and local training centers offer welder certification.

quiz.q: Why are welding codes important?
options: B) They prevent failures that can kill people
quiz.explanation: Welding codes ensure safety and prevent catastrophic failures.
